content: Vision loss refers to the complete or partial absence of vision that was previously present. This condition can occur suddenly (acutely) or develop gradually over time (chronically). The underlying causes of vision loss are diverse and may include abnormalities in the eye's refractive media, retinal diseases, optic nerve disorders, visual pathway disruptions, or functional disorders. In some cases, vision loss may also result from central nervous system abnormalities. Classification of Vision Loss To understand the underlying mechanisms and guide treatment, vision loss should be characterized based on its presentation: Unilateral or Bilateral: Whether one or both eyes are affected. Transient or Persistent: Whether the vision loss is temporary or long-lasting. Sudden or Gradual: The speed of onset. Painless or Painful: Whether the vision loss is associated with discomfort. Pathophysiology of Vision Loss Media Opacity Opacities in the eye's clear refractive media, such as the cornea, anterior chamber, lens, or vitreous humor, can lead to acute vision loss. This is often experienced as blurry vision or reduced visual acuity. While pupillary reflexes may be affected, these conditions typically do not cause a relative afferent pupillary defect. Common causes include: Corneal edema Hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber) Cataracts Vitreous hemorrhage Retinal Disease Diseases affecting the retina can result in sudden vision loss. These conditions often present with a relative afferent pupillary defect due to retinal involvement. Examples include: Retinal detachment Macular diseases, such as macular degeneration Retinal vascular occlusions, particularly central retinal artery occlusion Optic Nerve Disease Disorders of the optic nerve can cause acute vision loss. These conditions are often associated with an abnormal pupillary reflex and a relative afferent pupillary defect in unilateral cases. Examples include: Optic neuritis Retrobulbar neuritis Papillitis Papilledema Glaucoma Ischemic optic neuropathy Giant cell arteritis Hypoxia The eye is highly sensitive to oxygen deprivation. Hypoxia can cause dimming of vision, often described as a brownout or greyout, along with peripheral vision loss. This may occur due to: Visual Pathway Disorders Disruptions in the visual pathway, though rare, can lead to acute vision loss. Examples include: Homonymous hemianopia Cortical blindness Functional Disorders Functional vision loss refers to cases where no organic cause can be identified. Historically referred to as hysterical or malingering, this term acknowledges the physician's inability to objectively assess the patient's subjective visual experience. Causes of Vision Loss Transient Vision Loss (lasting less than 24 hours) Amaurosis fugax: Unilateral vision loss lasting minutes. Migraine: Vision loss lasting 10–60 minutes. Ocular ischemic syndrome: Associated with carotid occlusive disease. Papilledema: Bilateral vision loss lasting minutes. Vision Loss Lasting More Than 24 Hours Sudden, Painless: Welder's flash: Ischemic optic neuropathy: Rule out giant cell arteritis to prevent permanent damage. Retinal artery or vein occlusion Retinal detachment Optic neuritis Occipital lobe stroke (CVA) causing cortical blindness. Gradual, Painless: Cataracts Age-related macular degeneration Diabetic retinopathy Chronic corneal disease Open-angle glaucoma Optic neuropathy or atrophy Refractive errors Retinitis pigmentosa Painful: Patient's age Onset and progression of vision loss Presence of trauma Associated symptoms, such as headaches Medication use Medical history, including alcohol, drug, or tobacco use Physical Examination The eye examination should focus on: Treatment of Vision Loss Medical Therapy Systemic steroids for conditions such as: Temporal arteritis Optic neuritis Pituitary apoplexy Herpes zoster Non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy Aspirin for cavernous sinus thrombosis Antibiotics for infections Anticoagulation for vascular causes Cycloplegic agents and hypertonic saline ointment for corneal hydrops Surgical Interventions Corneal transplant for corneal hydrops. Surgical repair for retinal detachment. Cataract removal for advanced cataracts. Temporal artery biopsy and steroids for temporal arteritis.
